title: The Alphabet and Spelling
objective: Name English letters, decode simple words, and spell your own name aloud.
intro_md:
[L1: In this lesson you learn the names of the English letters so you can spell your name aloud and understand spelled words. Careful: English letter NAMES are not the same as their sounds, and several names are different from the letters you may know.]
{{l1_contrast:letter_names_vs_sounds}}
notes: Band file marks this lesson test_out: latin_script_l1 — Latin-script L1 learners may test out of the decoding half; the spelling-aloud half (ex 5-8) stays for everyone because letter NAMES differ even for Latin-script L1s. TODO_audio: exercises 2, 3, 5, 7 and the speaking model in ex 8 carry the spoken material as written transcript in the prompt; audio assets not yet produced.

exercises.rationale: Anchor the four metalanguage items first so every later instruction line ('spell the word') is comprehensible input, not noise.
E/I is the highest-stakes letter-name confusion for es (and pt) L1s: the English name of E is the sound es speakers write as 'i'. Getting this wrong corrupts every spelled name.

options.label: E
options.rationale: English E is named /iː/ — like the es letter 'i'.

options.label: I
options.rationale: es transfer: learners map the /iː/ sound to their letter 'i'. English I is named /aɪ/.

options.label: A
options.rationale: English A is named /eɪ/, which es ears parse as 'ei' — the second member of the same confusion triangle.

exercises.rationale: G/J is the second classic letter-name trap (band pron target P4): both names contain /dʒ/, and the es names of g/j invert the mapping.

options.label: G
options.rationale: Named /dʒiː/ — consonant /dʒ/ + the E-vowel from ex 2.

options.label: J
options.rationale: Named /dʒeɪ/ — same consonant, different vowel; es speakers often swap the two names wholesale.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Match the first letter to the word.]
exercises.rationale: Letter-to-word decoding using only known vocabulary; H and W have long, opaque English names that never resemble their sounds, so they need an early explicit anchor.

exercises.prompt: [audio] 'name' — [L1: Put the letters in order to spell the word you hear.]
exercises.rationale: First composition task: from spoken word to letter sequence. 'name' is the word the learner will spell about themselves for the rest of the course.

exercises.prompt: A: How do you spell 'word'?  B: W, O, R, ___.
exercises.rationale: Embeds spelling inside the real exchange it will occur in; final-position D/T discriminates the devoicing that es and vi ears apply to English final consonants.
Whole-word decoding from a spelled sequence — the skill needed when someone spells a name on the phone; the double L must actually be counted.

options.label: hello
options.rationale: Five letters, with the double L heard as 'L-L'.

options.label: hi
options.rationale: Same meaning, wrong form — catches learners who guess from context instead of decoding the letters.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Say your name, then spell it aloud, letter by letter.]
asr_focus: each letter name intelligible as a discrete unit
E vs I and G vs J names not swapped
vowel-letter names use English values, not L1 values
exercises.rationale: The survival act this lesson exists for (band P4: forms, phones); personalized production with ASR checking exactly the letter-name confusions trained in ex 2-3.
